Birds of the same species can experience very different mating success depending on the region they inhabit. In eastern regions, individuals often benefit from more stable climates, denser vegetation, and greater food availability, all of which contribute to healthier populations and more frequent social interactions. These conditions foster environments where birds are more likely to encounter potential mates, establish territories, and engage in courtship behaviors without as much environmental stress. Additionally, eastern habitats are sometimes more fragmented into smaller patches that concentrate birds, further increasing the likelihood of mating encounters.

In contrast, their western counterparts may face harsher or more variable climates, sparser vegetation, and lower population densities. These factors can spread individuals across larger areas, reducing the frequency of mate encounters and making territory establishment more difficult. Limited water and food sources can also divert energy away from reproduction. As a result, while the birds belong to the same species, those from the eastern regions generally have an ecological advantage that leads to more consistent and successful mating opportunities.
